articles.title: Tyler Perry has listed his Beverly Hills mansion for $57 million; the price tag puts his sprawling Hollywood property back in the luxury real estate spotlight
articles.summary: Tyler Perry is putting one of his most recognisable residential properties on the market, asking $57 million for his sprawling Beverly Hills estate.
articles.body: Tyler Perry is putting one of his most recognisable residential properties on the market, asking $57 million for his sprawling Beverly Hills estate. The listing, reported by The Wall Street Journal, Architectural Digest and Realtor dot com in September 2026, comes as the filmmaker and entertainment mogul prepares for a planned move to Puerto Rico. The gated property, which once provided temporary accommodation for Prince Harry and Meghan Markle, is among the high-profile celebrity homes attracting attention in the luxury real estate market. Perry’s mansion sits within the exclusive Beverly Ridge Estates community and spans approximately 24,600 square feet. The estate combines a Mediterranean-inspired residence with extensive grounds, offering a level of privacy and scale that has long defined the top end of Beverly Hills real estate.A sprawling estate with a royal connectionPerry acquired the land in 2004 for approximately $4.3 million and spent years developing the property, completing the mansion in 2012. The residence features eight bedrooms and 15 bathrooms, alongside generous living and entertainment spaces.The property became particularly well known in 2020, when Prince Harry and Meghan Markle stayed there after stepping back from their senior royal roles and relocating to California. Perry offered the couple a private place to stay during a period of transition, bringing further international attention to the estate.Beyond its celebrity associations, the property reflects Perry’s broader real estate investments. The filmmaker also owns a substantial Atlanta property connected to Tyler Perry Studios, a private island in the Bahamas and a Wyoming estate that was listed for $39.5 million earlier in 2026.Inside the Beverly Hills mansionThe house was designed around a Mediterranean aesthetic, with expansive interiors and carefully landscaped grounds. Its layout includes multiple living and entertaining areas, a library, a home theatre, a game room, a music room and a wine cellar. A separate guesthouse and staff accommodation add to the estate’s scale.The grounds, which extend across more than 22 acres according to published reports, provide considerable separation from neighbouring properties. The gated setting and secluded location have helped make the estate particularly suited to buyers seeking privacy alongside proximity to Los Angeles.The $57 million asking price reflects both the size of the residence and its position in one of the region’s most exclusive residential communities. However, the listing price does not guarantee a sale at that figure, particularly in a luxury market where negotiations can produce substantial differences between asking and closing prices.Celebrity real estate continues to command attentionPerry’s listing arrives amid a series of high-value transactions involving celebrities and entertainment industry figures. These deals show how homes can become significant assets in their own right, with location, land, architectural design and amenities often contributing as much to their appeal as their owners’ fame.Ellen DeGeneres and Portia de Rossi sold their approximately 10-acre Carpinteria estate for $96 million in 2024, according to The Wall Street Journal and Realtor dot com. The oceanfront property included a main residence, a guest cottage and a cabana, making it one of the most notable celebrity-related residential transactions of that year.Media entrepreneur Byron Allen sold a full-floor condominium at New York’s 220 Central Park South for $82.5 million in March 2025. The off-market deal, reported by The Wall Street Journal, highlighted the continued appetite for trophy properties in Manhattan’s Billionaires’ Row. Other headline-making sales include British singer Robbie Williams’ Beverly Hills-area estate, which rapper Drake acquired in 2022 for a reported price in the mid-$70 million range, according to the Los Angeles Times. articles.summary: A box of old medals bought for just £25 at a car-boot sale in West Yorkshire, England, has turned into an unexpected discovery for its buyer.
articles.body: A box of old medals bought for just £25 at a car-boot sale in West Yorkshire, England, has turned into an unexpected discovery for its buyer. One of the 22 medals inside was found to be a rare piece made in memory of British explorer Captain James Cook, who died in 1779. The medal was eventually sold for £5,000 at an auction in May. Its new owner is a museum in Whitby, which plans to put it on display during a special exhibition in 2028.The man who initially bought the medals had no idea how valuable this particular medal was. According to Tennants Auctioneers, which later handled the sale. The box contained 22 medals from different periods, with some dating back to the 18th century and others belonging to the 20th century.After going through his purchase, he noticed that one of the medals featured Captain James Cook and suspected it might be worth keeping. He sold the remaining medals for a combined £500, already making considerably more than he had spent on the box.But the biggest surprise was still to come. The man took the Cook medal to Tennants Auctioneers to have it examined. Specialists there identified it as an unusually rare commemorative medal from the 18th century. They estimated that it could sell for between £3,000 and £4,000, but the actual selling price turned out to be even higher.Why was the Captain Cook medal so rare?The medal was made to commemorate Cook's death in 1779. He was killed on February 14 that year following a dispute with Native Hawaiians at Kealakekua Bay.The bronze medal has a portrait of Cook on it and is believed to be among the earliest pieces produced to mark his death.According to Tennants, examples of this particular medal rarely come up for auction. The auction house said only two examples were listed in museum collections when it examined the piece.One is part of the National Maritime Museum's collection in Greenwich, London. The other is held by the Powerhouse Collection in Sydney, Australia.Tennants announced the discovery on April 13, ahead of its Coins and Banknotes Sale.Museum pays £5,000 for the medalWhen the medal was offered at Tennants on May 6, it sold for £5,000 to Captain Cook Memorial Museum in Whitby, which wanted to add the rare piece to its collection.The museum's interest was connected to an exhibition planned for 2028, the year marking the 300th anniversary of Cook's birth.The exhibition will take place in a building with a direct connection to the explorer's younger years. Located beside the harbour in Whitby, the museum occupies the building where Cook once lived while working as an apprentice.Richard Kornicki, Chairman of Trustees at the Captain Cook Memorial Museum, said, "This is a major acquisition for a volunteer-run Museum with no public funding; it will be displayed in the harbourside building where the young James Cook lived as an apprentice as part of a special exhibition to reflect on the legacy of his remarkable life and achievements.You use AI every day. articles.title: Healey vows cheaper marmalade and gherkins in pre-Budget package
articles.summary: The chancellor will axe tariffs on some staples as part of plans to give households "breathing space".
articles.body:
John Healey will remove import taxes on marmalade, gherkins and more than 100 products in a bid to give families "breathing space" with the cost of living at the Budget .

The chancellor on Wednesday will promise a fresh series of "everyday fixes" to ease the pressure on households.

The measures will also include an end to the so-called cliff-edge for those receiving carer's allowance payments and higher tax-free mileage rates being made permanent.

But the Conservatives said the offer of "cheaper gherkins" was "an insult to families hammered by Labour's tax rises".

Ahead of the Budget, the government said it is removing tariffs on more than 100 "family favourite" products, while supporting farmers facing higher fertiliser costs and households reliant on heating oil.

The government says the changes could save households up to £21 per year when combined with existing tariff suspensions on products including pasta, fruit juice and tuna.

Healey's Budget needs to sustain the stronger economy through gathering clouds

Marmalade, for example, will see a 20% tariff, plus an additional £19 charge per 100kg imported, suspended.

Healey said the ongoing wars in Iran and Ukraine had "hit families here at home through higher everyday costs".

"We can't control global events, but we can act where we can make a difference," he added.

Other measures the government announced include:

Making permanent a 55p per mile tax-free mileage rate for those driving up to 10,000 miles for work, with the rate rising from 25p per mile to 35p above that

Allowing carers to earn more than an existing earnings limit without losing their entire allowance, replacing it with a taper mechanism instead

Giving two weeks of paternity pay to self-employed fathers, who have previously missed out on payments of up to £194 a week for the period

And rolling out hundreds of additional Post Office drop boxes to make sending parcels easier

The government will also freeze fuel duty again in the Budget, the BBC understands.

As first reported in The Sun, the 5p duty discount is also set to continue. That discount was first introduced in 2022, and was due to last 12 months, but has been extended ever since.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham said: "We are taking on the big challenges facing the country. But that doesn't mean losing sight of the everyday problems that cost people money or simply aren't fair.

"If you're a nurse driving for work, a parent spending those precious first weeks with your new baby, or an unpaid carer picking up an extra shift, these changes will make life a little easier and put more money back in your pocket."

But the Conservatives said Burnham's "everyday fixes" have already been wiped out by higher borrowing costs, taxes and inflation.

Shadow chancellor Andrew Griffith said: "Shoppers face rising costs at the till and families are struggling to make ends meet, but Burnham's plan is cheaper gherkins. This is an insult to families hammered by Labour's tax rises."

articles.title: SC to UP police: Educate officers on investigation
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: In a severe indictment of Uttar Pradesh police for carrying out a “slipshod investigation” that resulted in a man being in custody for six
articles.body: NEW DELHI: In a severe indictment of Uttar Pradesh police for carrying out a “slipshod investigation” that resulted in a man being in custody for six years when there was no evidence against him, Supreme Court Monday said the state cannot shirk its responsibility to protect citizens and directed it to pay a compensation of Rs 6 lakh to him.“This is a classic case of how an investigation should not be proceeded with, resulting in the prosecution putting into jeopardy a person’s life and liberty,” SC noted at the outset of its verdict.On Sept 30, in a separate matter, the top court had slammed UP police for not naming the accused in a road accident case.Appalled at the way UP cops carried out probe: SCIt would be better if investigations in all criminal cases were handed over to CBI if the state police works with an agenda and does cover-up jobs, court had said, noting the accused had not been named despite the complainant catching him on the spot and handing him over to police.In the present case, a bench of J B Pardiwala and K Vinod Chandran said there was no evidence to implicate the person in a kidnapping and murder case. It noted he was never named in the FIR and police made him an accused on the basis that he was seen in CCTV footage. SC said it was “appalled at the manner in which investigation was carried out”. “It is unfortunate that despite no evidence against the petitioner, he was imprisoned for six years as an undertrial. Based on a slipshod investigation, a haphazard prosecution was carried out, which resulted, fortunately, in the acquittal of the accused. We cannot but deprecate the manner in which the probe was carried out and prosecution conducted,” SC said. “State police would do well to educate their officers in the process of investigation.”Making the state accountable for police’s misdeed, the court said six years have been erased from the man’s life on the strength of a concocted story built on mere surmises and conjectures, and the state has to pay compensation.“The state cannot shirk from its responsibility to protect its citizens, especially when a person arraigned in a criminal case is presumed innocent until proven guilty. The investigation and prosecuting agencies exist not merely to, and by whatever means, bring in a conviction. They should recognise themselves to be essential stakeholders in the justice delivery system, ensuring justice, not only to the victim, the de facto complainant and the injured but also to the accused,” the SC bench said.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: More than a third of deaths of ex-prisoners in Wales drug related - report
articles.summary: Politicians are being urged to tackle "systematic failures" in the criminal justice system.
articles.body:
More than a third of deaths of former prisoners on probation in Wales in a year were drug related, according to a new report.

The Wales Governance Centre at Cardiff University, which has published the report, is urging politicians to tackle "systematic failures" in the criminal justice system.

The deaths figure is higher than the proportion recorded across England and Wales as a whole, where deaths in this category accounted for just over a fifth of the total.

Report author Dr Robert Jones called on the UK and Welsh governments to find a solution to the "tragic" situation.

The Welsh government said it was working to reduce "harms caused by substance misuse".

The UK government said it was spending £3.4m on services to help support prison leavers overcome addiction.

According to the report, 37% of all deaths among prison leavers supervised by probation in Wales in 2024-25 were drug related.

The number of drug poisonings where the intent was "undetermined" in Wales accounted for 19 of the 52 who died.

Jones said this was "substantially higher" than the proportion across England and Wales as a whole, where deaths in this same category accounted for just over a fifth (21%) of the total - 131 out of 620.

Criminal justice in Wales is controlled by Westminster.

The Plaid Cymru Welsh government, and the previous Labour administration in Cardiff before it, argue it should be devolved.

Speaking to BBC Wales, Jones said the research looked at UK government data including Freedom of Information requests.

He said: "The added shock value to this is that these data point towards some systematic failures with incredibly tragic circumstances and consequences.

"Yet there isn't really a particular debate or discussion ongoing at the moment about these deaths, and indeed their causes, and how we might actually find a solution to them."

Jones said many areas of social policy, including "responsibility for tackling substance use, housing, education and local government" were devolved to the Welsh government.

"So what tends to happen is that criminal justice matters can often fall between the gaps between debates in the Senedd and debates in Westminster," he added.

Jones said the report raised "important questions about the current devolution settlement and whether the Welsh government has the powers and levers necessary to address the underlying causes of many of the challenges facing Wales".

He added: "Only by confronting the realities highlighted throughout this report can politicians and policymakers hope to overcome the many challenges facing communities across Wales."

David Bennett, from Wallich, Wales's largest homelessness charity, claimed most drug-related deaths "are preventable if we treat drug use as a health, not criminal justice, issue".

"Housing, health and justice need a joined-up approach," he said.

He said the charity supported "conversations to devolve justice and policing" and said without "coordinated" support prison leavers were "being set up to fail".

"The war on drugs hasn't worked," he added.

The report also says homelessness among former prisoners in Wales is continuing to rise.

The number of people leaving prison, supervised by Welsh probation services, who were recorded as rough sleeping on the day of their release rose by 24% in 2025-26.

In total, 695 prison leavers managed by Welsh probation services were rough sleeping on the day of their release.

Other findings include that more than a third (39%) of all custodial sentences given to women in Wales in 2025 were for offences related to thefts from shops.

Meanwhile, people from black ethnic groups in Wales remained the most overrepresented ethnic group in the prison population in 2025.

There were 58 black people from Wales in prison for every 10,000 of the population, compared with 15 white people per 10,000 of the population.

A spokesperson for the Welsh government said: "Every drug-related death is a tragedy.

"We are working closely with health boards, local authorities, Public Health Wales and other key partners to reduce the harms caused by substance misuse, focusing on early intervention, prevention, treatment and recovery support."

They added that the findings "strengthen the case for the full devolution of justice to Wales".

"Bringing responsibility for justice into line" with devolved services "would enable a more effective and joined-up approach to improving outcomes, reducing reoffending and building safer communities across Wales", the spokesperson added.

A Ministry of Justice spokesperson said: "We inherited prisons in crisis but we're acting on all fronts, including by reducing the number of women in custody through investment in community services and cutting the flow of drugs into prisons.

"In Wales we invest more than £3.4m into services which work across prisons, probation and courts to help support prison leavers overcome their addiction."

They added that prisoners at risk of becoming homeless can be offered temporary accommodation by the prison and probation service.

articles.title: New weather warnings as third storm set to hit Scotland
articles.summary: The country is braced for the third storm in as many days as communities continue to clean up after the weekend.
articles.body:
Two new weather warnings have been issued as a third storm in a matter of days is set to batter Scotland.

It comes as thousands of homes across the country remain without power in the aftermath of Storm Boelo.

A yellow warning for wind covering the south-west of Scotland came into effect at 18:00 and runs until 03:00 on Tuesday.

A separate yellow wind warning, covering most of the country as well as parts of northern England and Northern Ireland, runs from 03:00 to 21:00 on Tuesday.

In pictures: Storm Boelo leaves a trail of destruction across Scotland

Tributes paid to man killed by falling tree in Storm Boelo

Thousands still without power after Storm Boelo batters Scotland

The Met Office said gusts of up to 65mph (105km/h) would hit coastal communities in the south-west on Monday evening and into the morning.

Forecasters added strong winds would be accompanied by heavy rain at certain points.

The latest weather system is unlikely to be as widely disruptive as Storm Boelo - or Storm Austen which came before it - and has so far not been named.

The next name on the storm list for the 2026/2027 season is Chloe.

Storm Boelo brought heavy flooding and wind gusts in some areas of up to 85mph (137km/h) on Monday.

A 60-year-old man died after being struck by a falling tree at Mid Kelton, near Castle Douglas, in Dumfries and Galloway on Sunday.

On Monday evening, Scottish and Southern Energy Networks (SSEN), which covers the north of Scotland, said work was ongoing to reconnect the supplies of about 15,000 homes that remained without power.

Meanwhile, Scottish Power Energy Networks (Spen) said all but a "very small number" of its 50,000 customers who lost power in Ayrshire and Dumfries and Galloway would have it restored by 02:00 on Tuesday.

Almost 100,000 homes had power restored in both areas across the weekend.

ScotRail said the "vast majority" of its services were running as normal.

However, it warned that speed restrictions would be in place on several routes until 16:00 on Tuesday due to heavy rainfall. They are:

Glasgow Queen Street/Edinburgh Waverley – Inverness

Glasgow Queen Street – Helensburgh Central

West coast ferry operator CalMac said many its services remained liable to disruption or cancellation at short notice and urged travellers to check its website for updates.

Passengers on NorthLink Ferries were advised that there was the "possibility of disruption" to services until Thursday because of the weather.

All schools and nurseries in the Western Isles will be shut until Wednesday at the earliest.

Ellon Academy will remain closed on Tuesday after being shut on Monday as a result of damage caused by the storm.

It comes after more than a dozen primary schools in Aberdeenshire and Rothiemay Primary School, in Moray, were closed on Monday due to a lack of power.

Twelve primary schools and nine nurseries across the Highlands were also subject to full or partial closures .

The Scottish Environment Protection Agency (Sepa) said it had put an amber risk of flooding in place for the northern and Western Isles and Caithness and Sutherland.

Sepa said areas of the southwest and Argyll, including the Solway Firth and Firth of Clyde, would experience volatile conditions, with large waves and strong winds.

They said flooding of low-lying land was likely.

Highland Council said flood gates on the mile-long Caol and Lochyside flood protection scheme, near Fort William, had been closed following a warning from Sepa.

Police Scotland said a high risk of disruption remained with poor weather conditions expected on Tuesday.

Police Scotland Assistant Chief Constable Mark Sutherland said that, although the amber weather warning was no longer in place, disruption was "likely well beyond that due to further poor weather, fallen trees and other damage caused by the storm".

Social Justice and Housing Secretary Shirley-Anne Somerville told BBC Scotland News there were "challenges ahead" due to the prolonged nature of the conditions.

She urged councils to review their readiness, adding authorities were working to ensure that "everything that can be done is being done".

Somerville also said that everyone can play a part by getting "households as resilient as we can, as well as looking after neighbours and friends".

articles.title: I'm one of a growing number of Gen Z birdwatchers - it helps my mental health
articles.summary: Caitlin Andrew hated birdwatching as a child but found a passion for it in her 20s.
articles.body:
"I would be such a grump," says Caitlin Andrew, recalling her teenage self on walks with her parents.

"They are both into birdwatching and they would stop and listen and look at things.

"We had some really nice walks and experiences, but I just didn't have an interest in them at the time. I do feel quite bad about it now."

Three years ago, during a difficult period in her life, Caitlin discovered birds offered an unexpected escape from her troubles.

She joined the growing number of young people flocking to birdwatching.

More stories from Glasgow & West Scotland

"I was 24 and living in Glasgow as a student," says Caitlin, who grew up in Midlothian.

"I had poor mental health and was feeling a bit low, and finding it quite difficult to connect to the world around me."

Around that time, Caitlin joined her family for a holiday on Islay.

The southern-most island of the Inner Hebrides is renowned for its wild birds, with more than 120 species to spot during the spring and autumn migrations .

"When we were there we did a lot of birdwatching," says Caitlin.

"And as you can imagine there are incredible things to see - choughs and white-tailed eagles."

Caitlin says, rather than feeling grumpy, she found a sense of peace and calm watching birds.

"Just taking time to look and listen and take in everything you are connected to the environment you are in."

Her parents were delighted when she asked for a pair of binoculars for her birthday.

But making her first forays into birdwatching, Caitlin felt no-one else shared her passion for birds.

"I did feel a little bit embarrassed to say I was doing it," she says.

"It is a stereotype, isn't it? It's associated with older people with a sedate life and picking it up in retirement - all things which I don't think are negative at all.

"But among my peers I was certainly the only person doing it properly in any kind of capacity."

Caitlin, who is a Gaelic speaker, found she was far from alone as a young female birdwatcher when she made a BBC Alba documentary about her hobby .

She came across an Inverness chapter of the Feminist Bird Club - a group founded in New York in 2016 to help make the interest inclusive and safe.

Caitlin also met female professionals and volunteers involved in bird conservation.

She says: "In the birdwatching community, everyone is so friendly and happy to tell you they have something interesting in their scope or have seen something interesting."

Research carried out for the RSPB suggests there are more than four million birdwatchers in Britain, up from 2.7 million eight years ago.

The number of Gen Z enthusiasts - people aged 16 to 29 - rose from an estimated 61,000 in 2018 to 724,000 today, according to the study.

"I love seeing crested tits in the Cairngorms. They are rare, so its a special thing to see them," she says.

"I'm always happy to see a gannet. They are big and so powerful. They're like dinosaurs."

Caitlin enjoys how different birds signal changes in the year.

"When you start to hear a chiffchaff in maybe March or April you know spring is coming, and that is really exciting," she says.

"And then when coming into winter there are redwings and fieldfares.

"It feels like these creatures are giving you pointers that things are changing, and it's lovely to connect to that."

She adds: "Life can be so turbulent. Things go and down and you never know what's coming - the political nonsense and all the rest of it.

"And these little animals, they are just all about finding food, raising babies, fledging their young and then doing it all again - they're just trying to survive.

"It does make your problems feel very small."

articles.title: Jordan strikes Syria after church attack, killing at least seven people
articles.summary: Syria closes border crossings with Jordan after air strikes kill seven people in Deraa and Suweyda, including children.
articles.body:
Jordan has carried out air strikes in Syria in retaliation for last week’s deadly church attack , with Syrian authorities saying the raids killed at least seven people, including three children and a woman.

The attacks on Monday prompted Syria to close its main crossing with Jordan.

Jordan’s Armed Forces said in a statement that it targeted “hideouts” of armed groups in southeastern Syria in “retaliation” for the gun attack at a church in its Karak governorate on Friday. At least nine people were killed and dozens more wounded in the shootings.

The Jordanian military said the strikes on Syria were launched “in coordination with the Syrian government”.

It said the raids “resulted in the killing and wounding of many members of these terrorist groups and the destruction of a number of their vehicles”.

Syria, however, denied any coordination with Jordan.

In a statement, the Syrian government said “the military operation was conducted without prior coordination or notification” and said it has launched an investigation into the attacks.

Syria’s Civil Defence service said at least four sites in rural Deraa and Suweyda provinces were hit on Monday evening, and that its crews had recovered the bodies of seven people: three men, a woman and three children.

Five of the dead – a man, a woman and three children – were members of one family killed in a strike on a tent in the village of Al-Tai in Deraa Province, the service said. Three other family members, including a child, were wounded.

A second strike hit Al Shayyah, also in Deraa, killing an 80-year-old man. A third hit a residential building in Muzayrib, in the Ain al-Basal area of Deraa, causing no casualties.

A fourth struck a residential building in the town of Shahba in Suweyda province, killing a 60-year-old man.

After the strikes, Syria’s border authority closed the Nassib crossing, suspending traffic in both directions. Nassib is the only crossing for passengers and commercial goods between Jordan and Syria.

A Syrian Foreign Ministry official called the strikes a “treacherous attack” and told Al Jazeera that the ministry would try to manage the fallout in a way that preserved Syrian sovereignty.

Earlier on Monday, Jordanian security forces arrested two brothers and their brother-in-law on suspicion of involvement in the church attack. The arrests took place in the village of Al-Jadeeda, after a shootout with authorities.

A Jordanian government source told Al Jazeera that the suspects sustained serious injuries during the confrontation, which lasted for about three hours.

The arrests and air strikes in Syria come after Jordan’s King Abdullah II pledged a stern response to the church attack. During the attack, three gunmen opened fire on mourners at a funeral in a Greek Orthodox church in Karak, about 90km south of the capital, Amman.

The king said those responsible would face the “harshest penalties” and ordered a review of the country’s security procedures.

Karak is home to a minority Christian population, which makes up about 300,000 of Jordan’s 11.5 million people.

articles.title: DUP MLA joins Carla Lockhart's calls for First Minister removal
articles.summary: Diane Forsythe backs Carla Lockhart and says there must be "profound consequences" for Sinn Féin.
articles.body:
A Democratic Unionist Party (DUP) assembly member has joined MP colleague Carla Lockhart's calls for Stormont's First Minister Michelle O'Neill to be "removed from office".

Diane Forsythe said "profound consequences" pledged over the Sinn Féin vice-president's handling of the Drumcree parading dispute "must be honoured".

Lockhart last week stepped down from the DUP's officer board in response to party leader Gavin Robinson not removing their deputy first minister to force O'Neill from the joint office.

It follows unionist anger over the first minister's involvement in protests on the Garvaghy Road , which blocked a contentious Orange Order parade from passing along the mainly nationalist street in Portadown, County Armagh.

O'Neill and several other senior Sinn Féin figures have been interviewed by police investigating the demonstrations, with unionists accusing the party of acting unlawfully.

The Sinn Féin deputy leader has defended her attendance at the demonstrations last month, saying she would "continue to stand with the Garvaghy Road residents".

The political row has sparked differences of opinion over how to respond within the DUP, which shares power with Sinn Féin in Stormont's devolved government.

Forsythe is an assembly member for the South Down constituency and part of the DUP's party officer team.

In a post on Facebook on Monday night, Forsythe said she was "pleased" to show her support for Upper Bann MP Lockhart at a recent rally in Portadown .

She accused Sinn Féin of "arrogance" and described the feelings of anger in the unionist community over O'Neill's actions as "immense".

"There have been commitments made to deliver profound consequences and that it cannot be business as usual. These must be honoured," she added.

"It is my view that Michelle O'Neill should be removed from office. The assembly and other ministerial offices would continue until the next election."

Forsythe added that in the absence of such "meaningful action", official engagements as first minister through the joint Executive Office should be stopped immediately as a "bare minimum".

Last week Robinson said he was "sorry" to see Lockhart quit the DUP's officer board but added that she remained "a key part of our team".

Speaking on the BBC's The View programme, the DUP leader said the party had reached a democratic decision on how to deal with the Drumcree fallout.

He questioned whether it was necessary to "punish everyone in Northern Ireland when actually we should be punishing those who broke the law".

"We have considered all options and we keep all options on the table," he added.

articles.title: Jio Platforms IPO: India's largest share sale could end cheap mobile internet for millions
articles.summary: Jio's IPO promises a windfall for investors, but could signal the end of cheap mobile data for millions.
articles.body:
India's biggest telecom giant, the Meta and Google-backed Jio Platforms, is set to make its stock market debut on Wednesday.

Despite a bruising spell for Indian markets, its historic $3.2bn initial public offering (IPO) - the country's largest ever - has drawn overwhelming demand from top global fund managers, domestic institutions and mom-and-pop retail investors.

Bids outstripped the shares on offer within hours of subscriptions opening on 21 October.

Owned by Asia's richest man, Mukesh Ambani, Jio is one of India's most consequential companies, with half a billion people subscribing to its cheap mobile data. But its meteoric rise has also been dogged by controversy.

The company burst onto India's crowded telecom scene in 2016, offering throwaway tariffs that got millions of Indians hooked to the internet.

But its launch led to a huge disruption in the telecom sector. A market once crowded with 17 operators shrunk to an oligopoly of just three, with critics accusing the deep-pocketed company of waging a price war that pushed rivals out of business.

More recently, Elon Musk criticised Ambani, calling him the "real boss of India", suggesting that Jio was trying to thwart Starlink's entry into India. Reliance dismissed the allegations saying it welcomed competition ‌from Musk.

For all the scrutiny it has faced over the last decade, Jio's discounted data plans have been a bedrock of India's digital revolution , spawning a huge digital economy and democratising online payments, food delivery and e-commerce in Asia's third-biggest economy.

Within three years of its launch, customer data usage rose fifty-fold and data prices crashed.

This aggressive discounting helped Jio rapidly amass some 553 million mobile subscribers by 2026. It also cemented its dominance in other segments, capturing 50% of the wireless broadband market and more than 40% of fixed broadband.

Jio also carries 60% of India's wireless data traffic and boasts of the largest 5G subscriber base outside China, according to brokerage Emkay Global, which has described the company as the "digital engine of India".

But analysts say its stock market debut - which will see its promoters dilute their shareholding by about 3% - could mark a turning point in Jio's pricing strategy, potentially bringing an end to years of ultra-cheap tariffs.

"The era of Jio using cheap tariffs as a market-share weapon is drawing to a close," said Nitya Shah, co-founder of KamayaKya Wealth Management.

"A listed Jio must answer to minority shareholders… which structurally reduces its incentive to keep pricing suppressed."

Jio's future growth will no longer be driven primarily by adding subscribers through discounted plans. Instead, it will depend on "earning more per subscriber - through the migration to 5G, successive tariff revisions, and the extension of fixed wireless broadband into homes fibre has never reached", brokerage company Motilal Oswal said in a note.

The listing could also pave the way for Jio's competitors to raise prices, as fears of being undercut by a cheaper rival begin to recede.

"The biggest beneficiary of this shift could be Vodafone Idea," says Shah. "It is a moment the sector's weakest balance sheet gets its strongest tailwind".

For Indian consumers, any further increases would come on the heels of an industry-wide tariff hike a few years ago. Analysts say another round of price rises could trigger a fresh churn in the market as price-sensitive customers switch to the cheapest plans available.

While consumers may have to brace for higher bills, Jio's IPO offers investors a bet on India's seemingly insatiable appetite for data - and the growing ecosystem of digital services the company offers across entertainment, cloud computing, gaming and financial services.

India has emerged as the second-largest consumer of mobile data in the world, driven by lower tariffs and rising penetration of smartphones.

Jio's monthly data use per customer has climbed from 28.7 GB in 2024 to 42.3 GB in 2026 - up by 52% in two years. As per some estimates, usage is expected to surge further to 65GB by the end of this decade as disposable incomes rise.

All of this will give a tailwind for Jio to drive long-term growth in average revenue per user.

"Penetration of most digital services remains well below China and the US, which leaves significant headroom [for growth]," according to Emkay Global.

The listing is also likely to enhance transparency and provide investors with a "clearer market valuation" for the company, according to Moody's rating agency, as Jio is currently part of Reliance Industries, which has businesses spanning oil refining and retail.

But as much as its central and growing role in India's economy has excited investors, the buzz about the IPO also comes from the fact that this is the first share sale from the Reliance conglomerate in over two decades.

The company - which started as a small spice and polyester yarn trading venture in 1958 before expanding into textiles, petrochemicals, refining and eventually to retail, telecom and digital services - is known for its track record of long-term wealth creation, and enjoys legendary status among mom-and-pop investors.

Dhirubhai Ambani , the founder of the Reliance empire, is said to have played a foundational role in popularising equity investing and taking it beyond the preserve of traders and wealthy families in the 1980s and 90s.

In its early years, Reliance built a vast base of individual shareholders by turning its annual general meetings into grand spectacles of big announcements, dividend payouts and celebrations of public share ownership. Over time, this helped forge a fiercely loyal investor base, many of whom developed a deep emotional bond with the company.

And while Reliance Industries' stock has fallen nearly 20% over the past year, its longer-term track record continues to inspire confidence.

"The company has given average annualised returns of around 30% consistently for thirty years," Kranthi Bathini of Mumbai-based WealthMills Securities told the BBC.

"That's why there's anticipation that the same magic can be replicated with the Jio IPO."

articles.title: El-Sayed voters call guaranteed income programs a good idea after the progressive signaled his support
articles.summary: Supporters of Michigan Democratic U.S. Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed voiced support for guaranteed income at a Detroit rally featuring former President Barack Obama.
articles.body: DETROIT – Supporters of Michigan Democratic U.S. Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed voiced support for guaranteed income, a social safety net concept gaining traction in municipalities across the nation. "I think it's a good idea," one rallygoer told Fox News Digital. "With the prices rising and programs being cut like they are and trying to get access to them. Yeah, I think it's a good idea. I hope he supports them." Fox News Digital spoke with voters outside Cass Technical High School in Detroit, where El-Sayed hosted a campaign rally featuring former President Barack Obama. The event marked a key moment in the progressive candidate’s effort to strengthen ties with the Democratic establishment as he seeks to succeed retiring Sen. Gary Peters, D-Mich. OBAMA PREPARES TO RALLY WITH MICHIGAN DEM WHO ONCE DELIVERED SCATHING VERDICT ON HIS PRESIDENCY Rallygoers leaving the overflow venue were asked whether guaranteed income programs are an effective policy and whether El-Sayed should make them a core pillar of his campaign. "I do, and I think the billionaires should be paying for it," voter Dave told Fox News Digital. Kiana Montgomery, a publicist, also voiced support for the concept — provided strict parameters are attached. "I do [support it]. I think there should be parameters — exactly what people can spend it on to ensure everybody's trying to uplift the community as a whole," Montgomery said. "A rising tide lifts all ships, and if people are in need, we should definitely support them." CALIFORNIA MAYOR INSISTS CASH HANDOUT PROGRAM WILL SOLVE AFFORDABILITY CHALLENGES, BUT CRITICS QUESTION COST El-Sayed has previously signaled support for direct-cash poverty interventions, including during an appearance at the "Guaranteed Income Now" summit in Detroit. However, his campaign platform focuses primarily on universal healthcare through Medicare for all, raising the minimum wage and expanding existing federal safety net programs. "How do we address poverty at that transition between generations in a family? We’ve got too many parents trying to do the impossible: to go to school, to raise kids, and to earn a living all at the same time," El-Sayed said at the summit. "So what we’ll be proposing ... in Wayne County is a pilot to invest $500 a month in young parents who are enrolled in community college," he added. "As you try to do the impossible, we can give you a leg up — one less shift of work a week to try and be that student you want to be and that parent that you need to be for your kids." The summit was hosted by the Economic Security Project (ESP), an advocacy group founded in 2016 by entrepreneurs, activists and researchers that has helped launch more than 100 guaranteed income pilots nationwide. Guaranteed income initiatives are typically structured as temporary, no-strings-attached pilot programs designed to measure the economic and health impacts of direct cash support. EXCLUSIVE: MICHIGAN HOUSE SPEAKER CALLS FOR ANSWERS OVER $300M TAXPAYER-FUNDED RX KIDS PROGRAM The debate over cash assistance comes as "Rx Kids"— a high-profile public-private cash aid initiative for expectant mothers and infants — expands across Detroit and other Michigan cities. The program provides eligible pregnant women with a one-time, unconditional $1,500 payment, followed by $500 per month for up to 12 months after birth. While Rx Kids organizers classify the model as a targeted "child allowance" rather than traditional universal basic income, critics argue that both rely on direct cash transfers. Michigan House Republicans have questioned the initiative's oversight and spending, which has secured nearly $400 million in combined public and philanthropic funding. House Oversight Committee Chairman state Rep. Jay DeBoyer, R-Clay Township, criticized the program's lack of spending guardrails, arguing that unconditional cash operates as a "redistribution of wealth" rather than a solution to systemic poverty. Republican lawmakers have raised concerns over transparency and administrative costs, noting that GiveDirectly, the nonprofit administering the program, receives tens of millions of dollars in fees. Conservative policy groups and state Republicans argue unconditional cash programs undermine workforce participation and deepen government dependency. Proponents, meanwhile, point to data from more than 250 cash transfer pilots across 40 states and Washington, D.C., arguing that direct cash transfers can reduce infant poverty and improve health outcomes. Detroit is among more than 100 U.S. municipalities that have experimented with basic-income-style pilots since 2018. As temporary federal COVID-19 relief funds have dried up, local leaders are searching for alternative ways to fund cash transfers permanently. In Cook County, Illinois, commissioners allocated $7.5 million in local taxpayer funding to continue the county's guaranteed income program as a permanent budget initiative. AS AMERICANS ARE CRUSHED BY AFFORDABILITY, GROWING TREND OF MAYORS PUSHING CASH HANDOUTS AS THE ANSWER For many rallygoers interviewed, economic support and healthcare access were closely connected. "He absolutely should [campaign on it], especially being a woman and knowing what women risk, especially in healthcare, how there's already a deference against us," supporter Tammy Bacon told Fox News Digital. "They don't listen to what we need. There's a significant need for women in healthcare and to listen to our issues, our values, and respect us and give us the care that we need without being discriminatory or presumptuous." Another supporter, Mohammed, a resident of Bloomfield Hills, agreed that targeted assistance could be effective if managed properly. "It's a good thing — as long as the money is being used the right way for good and for children … women, children, and pregnant women," Mohammed said. "For people who want to get an education, that's a good idea, too." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP El-Sayed’s campaign did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital’s request for comment.

articles.title: West Virginia couple charged after kids found in alleged ‘house of horrors’

articles.body: A West Virginia couple is facing felony charges after authorities said three children endured years of alleged abuse and neglect inside what the local sheriff described as a real-life "house of horrors." Erica Lynn Sayre, 45, and her husband, Clifford Gale Sayre, 46, both of Evans, were charged following an "extensive investigation" by the Jackson County Sheriff's Department, authorities announced Monday. Erica and Clifford Sayre each face six felony charges, including three counts of child neglect creating risk of injury. Erica Sayre also faces three counts of child abuse resulting in bodily injury, while Clifford Sayre faces three counts of child neglect resulting in bodily injury. Authorities alleged the children were repeatedly struck and strangled, deprived of food and water and denied access to the bathroom. TENNESSEE INMATE CONVICTED OF MURDER ESCAPES FROM PRISON, MANHUNT UNDERWAY: OFFICIALS Investigators also alleged that soiled cat litter was dumped in their beds, dog feces was placed on their belongings and they were forced to run barefoot on a gravel driveway as punishment. The children were also allegedly struck with household objects, forced to put a soiled sock in their mouths and subjected to having their hair forcibly cut. "One child described being struck in the head with an electronic device, causing a bleeding injury for which she was denied medical treatment. One of the children was threatened to be killed if she contacted Child Protective Services," the sheriff's office alleged. During interviews, one child became emotional and told investigators, "I can't go back to that home," the sheriff's department said. Another said she "just wants a normal life." TEEN ACCUSED OF STEPSISTER’S CRUISE SHIP MURDER BUYS TIME TO CONSIDER PLEA BUT WON’T GET ‘SWEET’ DEAL: EXPERT Investigators alleged Clifford Sayre witnessed repeated abuse but failed to intervene. One child claimed he restrained her hands while Erica Sayre cut her hair with a razor blade, causing an injury. "Because mom hits us and Gale lets her," the children said during a forensic interview, according to the sheriff's department. Authorities said investigators worked with Child Protective Services and a Child Advocacy Center and documented scars that were consistent with portions of the children's accounts. Investigators said the children's statements also corroborated one another and other physical evidence collected during the investigation. All of the children were removed from the home after the allegations were disclosed, according to authorities. The investigation included multiple interviews, medical examinations and photographic evidence. "The Jackson County Sheriff's Department emphasizes the seriousness of allegations involving child abuse and neglect of vulnerable children and remains committed to investigating such reports thoroughly and efficiently," Sheriff Ross Mellinger said in a statement. articles.title: Delaware sank a retired 180-foot fishing vessel in August 2026 after it was transferred for just $1; now it forms an artificial reef about 26 miles offshore, although no increase in fish populations has yet been measured
articles.summary: A retired 180-foot commercial fishing vessel was deliberately sunk off the Atlantic coast of Delaware in August 2026 to create an artificial reef.
articles.body: A retired 180-foot commercial fishing vessel was deliberately sunk off the Atlantic coast of Delaware in August 2026 to create an artificial reef. The new reef will provide habitats for marine life and create new locations for recreational diving. The vessel, named the F/V Calcasieu Pass, was sunk on August 12 at Delaware Reef Site 13. The site is about 26 miles offshore from the Indian River Inlet. The ship now rests at a depth chosen to attract different fish species and support ocean biodiversity. According to a press statement from seafood industry group Saving Seafood, the vessel was previously operated by commercial fishing company Ocean Harvesters. In 2024, the company transferred the retired ship to marine contractor Coleen Marine for a symbolic payment of $1. The goal was to turn the vessel into an artificial reef. Coleen Marine handled the preparation, towing and sinking process to ensure the vessel was placed safely and met environmental standards. Before the ship was released into the Atlantic Ocean, crews removed hazardous materials, oil and loose debris as part of the required cleanup.Second life for retired industrial vesselThe F/V Calcasieu Pass first worked as a supply vessel for offshore oil fields. It was later converted into a commercial fishing boat used to catch menhaden. These small, nutrient-rich fish are mainly used to make fish meal, fish oil and other marine products for industrial use. In an official statement published by Saving Seafood, Ocean Harvesters Chief Executive Officer Monty Deihl discussed how retired ships can continue to help marine conservation efforts. "Retired working vessels can continue to provide value long after their fishing days are over," Deihl said. "We’re pleased to see the Calcasieu Pass begin a new chapter as marine habitat, supporting the ecosystem while creating new opportunities for anglers and divers." Artificial reefs provide solid structures on ocean floors that would otherwise be mostly flat and featureless. These steel structures give sport fish and other marine life places to hide, breed and find food. They also support organisms that attach themselves to hard surfaces and species that live on the seafloor.Monitoring ecosystem impact and fish stocksState wildlife officials and marine biologists expect the new reef to attract marine life, but monitoring is still underway. Early surveys carried out soon after the sinking have not yet recorded measurable increases in local fish populations at the site. According to Delaware environmental managers, artificial reefs need time to develop into complete ecosystems. Marine life such as algae, barnacles and mussels usually begins growing on the steel hull over several months. This growth can attract smaller fish that serve as prey, followed by larger predatory fish. State environmental agencies monitor artificial reef sites over several years. They track how quickly marine life settles in, whether the structures remain stable and how fish populations in the area change over time.Delaware expands offshore reef networkThe sinking of the Calcasieu Pass adds another site to Delaware's network of artificial reefs. State authorities manage these reefs along the Atlantic coast and within Delaware Bay. For several decades, Delaware has used retired ships, concrete structures, subway cars and surplus military equipment to expand its artificial reef programme. According to details released by Saving Seafood, using retired menhaden fishing vessels to build reefs follows an established regional practice. In 2020, Coleen Marine prepared and sank another former menhaden vessel, the Reedville, at a Delaware reef site. Similar projects took place off the coast of Mississippi in 2023. Retired fishing boats, including the F/V Mermentau and the F/V G.P. Chauvin, were sunk to strengthen marine habitats along the Gulf Coast. The Delaware Department of Natural Resources and Environmental Control continues to oversee artificial reef projects. The programme aims to support marine biodiversity along the coast, commercial fishing and eco-tourism. Recreational anglers and scuba divers can find the geographic coordinates for Reef Site 13 on state maritime charts. Authorities advise boaters to follow local navigation warnings when visiting the offshore site.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Portland officials say city did not approve policies that led to removal of women's sports supporters
articles.summary: Officials say the city of Portland is reviewing the Providence Park incident where women's sports supporters were struck and forcibly removed by security.
articles.body: Officials for the City of Portland says they are reviewing a filmed confrontation in which women’s sports supporters were struck and forcibly removed from a publicly owned soccer stadium. The city denied involvement in decisions concerning the spectators and an OutKick reporter, identifying the stadium operator and its subcontractors as responsible. It also said the operator’s agreement requires compliance with applicable laws. "The City is reviewing," officials told OutKick. "Decisions concerning the incident in question are handled by the Stadium Operator Peregrine, LLC and their subcontractors. The City was not involved in any decisions concerning the spectators or reporter." Asked whether the city approved policies governing XX-XY clothing, messages about transgender participation in sports, banners or press credentials, officials answered, "No." WNBA WON'T NAME PERSON RESPONSIBLE FOR SECURITY INCIDENT OVER FANS' SHIRTS, AS DREAM BLAME LEAGUE "The Stadium Operating Agreement requires the Operator to not only implement a Security, Safety and Traffic Control plan but also comply with all applicable laws. The Ticket Terms and Conditions require all spectators comply with all rules, regulations, and policies of the Thorns, the NWSL and Peregrine Sports, including the Providence Park Guest Guide." Asked what explanation the operator had provided for the removals, and whether the city was examining consistent enforcement across spectators expressing different views, officials said they were still seeking information. "The City is working with the Stadium Operator to receive more details about the incident," the response stated. The response comes as the Justice Department separately reviews the Oct. 23 incident at Providence Park for potential constitutional concerns. "The Justice Department is aware of these reports and will review the matter thoroughly. Where the facts and the law warrant action, the Department will not hesitate to act," a department spokesperson told OutKick. A Justice Department official said that, based on information available so far, the described conduct appears to raise viewpoint discrimination and First Amendment questions rather than sex discrimination. HOSTILE VALKYRIES FANS VERBALLY ATTACKED WOMEN'S SPORTS ACTIVISTS AT WNBA FINALS GAME 1 IN SAN FRANCISCO Friday’s confrontation began during the Portland Thorns’ match against the North Carolina Courage. Approximately 20 spectators kept their XX-XY Athletics shirts covered through the first half, then revealed them and displayed a large "Save Women’s Sports" banner at the start of the second half. Footage captured members of the group being struck by other spectators, including with flagpoles carrying transgender flags, and being forcibly escorted out by security. The organizers included activist Amy Sousa and commentator Brandi Kruse. WNBA ADMITS SECURITY IN ATLANTA WAS WRONG TO MAKE FANS COVER SHIRTS AT DREAM-FEVER GAME Officials cited Section 4 of the stadium operating agreement as the source of the operator’s authority, saying Section 4.3 requires implementation of a security, safety and traffic control plan. They said the agreement requires the operator to comply with applicable laws, while ticket terms require spectators to follow the policies of the Thorns, NWSL and Peregrine Sports, including the stadium’s guest guide. The response did not identify which provision security applied during Friday’s confrontation. Providence Park is city-owned and operated by Peregrine Sports. Portland’s Spectator Venues Program oversees the city’s interests in the facility and its relationship with the operator. The First Amendment generally restricts government action, and a private organization does not automatically become a government actor simply because it holds a public contract. But government direction or joint participation can bring private conduct under constitutional scrutiny. Portland also did not explicitly confirm whether it would request preservation of surveillance footage and incident reports or consider corrective action if misconduct or a contractual violation were established. articles.title: In 2026, Arizona officials rejected a data-centre plan covering 3,000 acres near Eloy; the developer had already reduced the proposed campus to 11 buildings
articles.summary: Arizona officials were set to decide on a proposed data centre development covering more than 3,000 acres of rural land near Eloy, after developer
articles.body: Arizona officials were set to decide on a proposed data centre development covering more than 3,000 acres of rural land near Eloy, after developer Vermaland reduced the planned campus by 80% following local opposition. The La Osa Energy Centre proposal includes 11 data centre buildings, an on-site gas-fired power plant and a battery energy storage system, with energy demand capped at 1 gigawatt. According to KJZZ, a National Public Radio (NPR) member station based in Phoenix, Arizona, the revised application also proposes limiting annual freshwater use to 600 acre-feet and introduces additional development conditions. The Pinal County Board of Supervisors was due to consider the rezoning request on 26 August 2026.Why was the Arizona data-centre plan rejected in 2026The revised proposal followed opposition from residents. At a public hearing in May 2026, Vermaland said it planned to reduce the scale of the development by 80% in response to community concerns. The revised zoning application specified that the company would not build more than 11 data centre buildings.KJZZ reported that, before the proposed reduction, La Osa would have been the largest planned data centre project in Arizona. The revised development remained among several large-scale data centre projects under consideration in the state. The developer also submitted 22 additional development conditions, which company officials said reflected feedback received during the lengthy May public hearing.What water limits applied to the La Osa data-centre projectThe revised application proposed limiting the site's use of potable, or fresh, water to 600 acre-feet annually. KJZZ explained that an acre-foot represents more than 300,000 gallons of water. The developer could seek to reduce or offset its freshwater consumption, including through the purchase of effluent water, but the county would not make such measures compulsory under the proposed conditions.The county would also receive annual reports detailing water use at the data centre campus and the on-site gas power plant. According to KJZZ, these reports could be shared with the public. The project's water use would additionally be subject to any conditions established by the final water provider. The revised proposal therefore included reporting requirements alongside the proposed annual limit on potable water consumption.How would the Arizona data centre meet its power needsVermaland stated that the development would generate its own electricity while waiting for a connection to the utility grid. The planned on-site gas power plant would have to comply with county-level emissions requirements. The developer also said it would pay the full cost of generating and delivering electricity to the site once the project was connected to the grid.However, KJZZ reported that enforcement of the commitment to cover those electricity costs would fall to the Central Arizona Irrigation and Drainage District, which was planning to serve the project. The application also included requirements for noise studies and provisions for decommissioning the battery storage facility after 24 months without use.What other data centre projects were planned in ArizonaLa Osa was not the only large data centre development being considered in Arizona. KJZZ reported that Maricopa County had approved more than 2,000 acres near Buckeye for a separate data centre project with a planned capacity of 1 gigawatt in 2025. The project was another example of the large-scale facilities being proposed in the state.In Page, residents were seeking to reverse the city council's sale of 500 acres near Horseshoe Bend to a developer planning another data centre with a proposed capacity of 1 gigawatt. The La Osa proposal, meanwhile, remained subject to the Pinal County decision on its rezoning and site planning request.KJZZ also clarified an error in an earlier version of its report. The original article had incorrectly stated that Pinal County had imposed dozens of conditions on the developer. The station subsequently corrected the report to explain that Vermaland had included the restrictions in its application.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: iPhone Duo: Apple says it will replace handsets with screen problems
articles.summary: Photos shared online showed faults appearing on the screens of Apple's first foldable device.
articles.body:
Apple says it will replace iPhone Duo handsets that have developed problems with their screens just days after the highly-anticipated smartphone went on sale.

Photos posted by social media users show lines that appeared on the screens of the technology giant's first ever foldable device , which has a starting price of £1,999 ($2,668) in the UK.

Apple said it is aware of "an issue impacting the inner display on a small number" of units and urged affected users to contact the company for a replacement.

The Duo's launch, which attracted long queues at Apple stores around the world last week, comes as the brand tries to reinvigorate its catalogue and challenge the foldable phones offered by rivals.

Some Duo owners also posted photos online showing cracks along the screen's centre crease, while others reported a crunching noise when opening the device.

The Duo's 7.6-inch (19.3cm) inner display is held together by a central hinge - a complex piece of engineering that has resulted in flaws in the folding devices made by some of Apple's competitors.

Samsung's first foldable phone, the Galaxy Fold, suffered an early setback in 2019 when reviewers reported broken screens on the devices.

articles.body: MS NOW anchor Peter Alexander asked Gov. Gretchen Whitmer, D-Mich., on Sunday whether Republican politicians were tapping into "xenophobia" ahead of the midterm elections. ROGERS FIRES BACK AT WELKER OVER EL-SAYED'S MUSLIM BROTHERHOOD CONTROVERSY, 'YOU ARE GIVING HIM A PASS' "Do you worry that there is some hidden xenophobia in Michigan right now that Donald Trump and Mike Rogers are trying to tap into?" Alexander asked. "I think that Mike Rogers and Donald Trump hope that there is, and that they're trying to cultivate that," Whitmer responded. articles.body: President Trump intensified attacks on Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed at a rally in Port Huron Sunday, calling him a “jihadist” who was “on the side of the terrorists” and questioning his loyalty to US. The remarks drew condemnation from a former Trump ally in the Arab American community.Trump said El-Sayed, a former Detroit health official, would “have to go through a metal detector before he’s allowed to go into Senate”. articles.title: My husband's death was hard enough - then came the admin
articles.summary: Louisa says her experience of dealing with household bills after her husband John died left her feeling "frustrated and angry".
articles.body:
Louisa Nicoll knew her husband John was going to die about a year before it happened. The couple used the time to make memories with their children, James and Amy, and John meticulously organised their paperwork.

But despite him asking for accounts to be switched to Louisa's name, she still received post addressed to him after his death. In one letter from their energy provider, it said: "Sorry you're leaving us. Is there anything we can do to make you stay?"

"I felt utterly exhausted, overwhelmed, frustrated and angry because of those experiences," she told BBC's Morning Live.

Louisa now campaigns for changes in the way companies deal with admin after someone dies and offers advice on how talking about death before it happens can help families cope afterwards.

John was 50 and working as a police surveillance trainer when he was diagnosed with cancer. Louisa had a career in palliative care nursing and was a ward manager in a hospice. John underwent nine major surgeries and four rounds of chemotherapy - working full-time through it all.

"He absolutely loved working with his supportive police colleagues, and he cherished everyday family life and spending time with our friends," says Louisa.

When further surgery was no longer an option, palliative chemotherapy was offered. Following many discussions, John decided to focus on making memories as a husband, dad and friend rather than spending his final months as a patient.

"He made a lovely speech at Amy's 18th birthday," she says. "We visited family in Scotland and had planned a family holiday to Greece - but Covid hit and we had a Greek night at home instead." The couple had a party for Louisa's 50th and their 25th wedding anniversary.

In the background, John was busy compiling a handover of the household admin.

"He even wrote a plan for me titled 'things you need to know', packed with every household account, insurance renewal and MOT dates," she says.

He had emailed their energy provider saying he would like Louisa to take over as the account holder due to his terminal diagnosis.

But instead, she was added as an additional name and had to close and reopen the account.

"I thought I was prepared for John's death but the reality was so much harder than I could ever have imagined. He really was the other half of me. So when I had to face the death admin, I felt so vulnerable without him beside me."

James and Amy's mobile phone contracts were in John's name, too. They were asked to take his death certificate into a store but still received texts that read "Hi, John".

"I'm sure nobody's doing this intentionally... but these companies could just get their bereavement services at a level that is not going to cause undue distress," says Louisa. "There should be a standardised practice."

Sarah Middlemiss, policy campaigns manager at end-of-life charity Marie Curie, tells Morning Live admin tasks can be particularly difficult when you are grieving.

"And because every company does things in a slightly different way and requires slightly different things, it can be really, really overwhelming," she says.

"Proper training on how to deal with people who are grieving or who are terminally ill in a really sensitive and timely manner would go a really long way."

Louisa gives talks at events to encourage people to talk about death in advance.

"We plan for every major event in life - weddings, pregnancy, career changes, retirement, even our meals each day - yet most people leave the end of life completely to chance," she says.

"Our families end up trapped in a crisis - guessing our wishes in the back of an ambulance or a chaotic A&E department."

She says she and John had those "hard but important conversations" long before they needed them.

John died peacefully at home in August 2020, just one day after their 26th wedding anniversary.

"Before he died, we spoke about what I would do for work after he died. He said, 'I think you'll tell our story, and show people that it is possible to live well when faced with dying.' And that is what I'm trying to do."
